course_description:
This course traces the rise of modern philosophy as a reaction to dramatic changes in scientific thinking in the seventeenth century. It examines three major points of intersection between science and philosophy in the period in debates about (1) the ontology of nature; (2) causation; and (3) cognitive psychology. Philosophers examined include Descartes, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, Spinoza, Malebranche, Margaret Cavendish, Ann Conway, Ralph Cudworth, Leibniz, Hobbes, Locke, Berkeley and Hume.

Many of the contemporary problems in philosophy and cognate fields have their roots in debates that began in the seventeenth century. What is the nature of matter? Is causation based on impetus? Is the unification of distinct sciences, like astronomy and physics, possible?ﾠWhat makes something alive? What does rational agency consist in? What role do the emotions play in our moral psychology and psychopathology?ﾠWhat are the origins of the State and what legitimacy does it have to coerce human activity? Does the State have a role to play in promoting the positive liberty of citizens, or should it only protect their negative liberties?ﾠ

With the demise of the dominant Aristotelian philosophy, questions such as these took on a new significance and demanded new ways of answering them. The search for cogent answers to these question has not stopped with the seventeenth century but continues today. Students in this course will, therefore, have an opportunity to understand the historical and philosophical foundations of some of the central debates of contemporary philosophy.ﾠ

The aims of this course are three: (1) to build students' knowledge of the central movements in the history of philosophy, (2) to demonstrateﾠthe continued relevance of these movements to the contemporary debates, andﾠ(3) to assist students in developing advancedﾠskills in argumentation.

course_aims: This course is the ultimate Bluffer's Guide to Philosophy, a course designed to ground a student's knowledge of philosophy in an understanding of the major shifts in philosophical thinking that occurred in the 17th century and serve as the origins of many contemporary philosophical debates. It builds on knowledge and skills developed in introductory philosophy courses: skills in philosophical analysis, argumentation and clarity of expression. Students will be able to expand on their knowledge of the contours of philosophical debates, working with more complex arguments and texts, and develop advanced argumentation and presentation skills.

learning_outcomes.description: Reflect and report on the philosophical and historical origins of central debates in philosophy.
Demonstrate advanced skills of effective thinking and communication.
Conduct independent philosophical research and inquiry.
Identify, analyse and evaluate complex arguments or points of view.
Develop an appreciation of diverse reasoned perspectives and engage in collaborative reasoning.

assessment_details.task_description: Tutorial work involves two components: (A) Tutorial participation (10%) and (B) 4x in-class activities (4 x 5%=20%). (Students with an accommodation must contact the course coordinator to arrange alternatives.) The first tutorial in week 1 reviews argument mapping, nutshell assignments, and asks students to complete a survey as part of a student-staff partnership. Graded tutorials run for the following 10 weeks minus week 3 (2; 4-12). Week 3 is the Ekka Holiday and there will be no tutorials that week either on Wednesday or Thursday. (A) Tutorial work enables steady development of skills in philosophical analysis and critical thinking. A Community of Inquiry approach is taken where students work together to solve problems. Students will be judged on their ability to work collaboratively to progress arguments, generate critical questions and prompts, and discuss competing interpretations and points of view. Tutorials are mandatory and attendance will be taken. Marks are not awarded for attendance but for contributions to collective discussion and completion of set tasks. Alternative or make-up work will be assigned to students who miss a tutorial due to documented medical or other legitimate reasons. During tutorials, students are expected to: 1. Demonstrate evidence of comprehension of the texts assigned for reading each week through preparation and participation in the tutorial. Required readings will be marked 'required' and made available through the Library. 2. Come to class with work prepared as assigned the week before each tutorial. This course integrates an optional use of Generative AI as part of the preparation for tutorials. 3. Conduct in-class analyses of short passages. (B) 4 x in-class activities are comprised of: Mini nutshell #1 (week 4) Socratic circle (week 5) Socratic circle (week 10) Pitch event (weeks 11 & 12) for research design task (See 'Research Design Task' below). Copies (e.g., photographs) of in-class work during these exercises must be uploaded by the student to the relevant Turnitin site at the end of the tutorial to obtain a grade. Recordings of in-class assessed work will be safely stored for up to 12 months as required by university policy. See Tutorial Participation and Exercises on Blackbaord for more information about these and other assessment tasks. Note on the use of AI: This assessment is designed to protect academic integrity and assess your understanding of course concepts. You must only use the approved materials and tools for this assessment task. Use of prohibited materials in this task may be investigated and treated as academic misconduct. assessment_details.title: Nutshell Argument Map #2
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific, Secure. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: In the Nutshell assignment (20%; 500 words) students are asked to contextualise, analyse, explain, and evaluate an argument contained in the text provided. Students will identify the structure of the argument (the relationship between premises and conclusion) in an argument map including the base argument and supporting reasons or hidden assumptions. Students will append a short statement contextualising the argument (i.e., situating it against an opposing view) and a short evaluation (identifying one major weakness or flaw in the argument). These are essential skills in the history of philosophy. This test will be conducted and submitted in 30 minutes during the lecture in week 6. Students will be informed of the text from which the argument is drawn in the week prior to the test. Criteria & Marking: Your nutshell assignments will be assessed according to the following criteria: 1. Ability to define the topic or philosophical issue under debate. (Topic definition.) 2. Ability to identify and analyse the structure of an argument for a certain conclusion. (Argument and Structure.) 3. Depth and breadth of understanding of the point at issue. (Scope and Depth of Treatment) 4. Insight and/or originality in analysing or argument. (Originality) 5. Capacity to produce a polished, well-written analysis and/or evaluation. (Presentation) Note on the use of AI: This assessment is designed to protect academic integrity and assess your understanding of course concepts. assessment_details.title: Research design task
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Select ONE topic from the Trialogue Task sheet available on Blackboard or design your own primary research question (with approval from the lecturers). Preparatory work for this assignment must be conducted in tutorials. Part A: Research design component (700 words total; 20%): Define the philosophical problem and key terms . (100 words) Generate secondary research questions . Either select a primary research question from the Trialogue Task Sheet or design your own (with approval from the lecturers). Label this 'RQ1'. To narrow your research focus, generate 2-3 secondary research questions related to specific aspects of the problem you are interested in investigating. Label these 'SRQ1', 'SRQ2', etc. Explain why these are significant and relevant secondary research questions to explore. (100 words) Locate 4 credible secondary sources reflecting different sides of the debate in the early modern period. Use the Library catalogue or Google Scholar to find sources. Read the articles to ensure relevance and significance. Cite the articles using APA7 and explain why each is relevant, significant, and credible. (See the CRAAP test for judging the credibility of sources). [NB: Secondary sources are articles or books written by scholars of early modern philosophy about the philosophical texts studied in this course.] (4 x 50 words per entry (excluding the citation) = 200 words in total.) Design a strong thesis statement . (50 words) Create an argument map of your trialogue. (250 words) Part B: Pitch event (3 minutes; 5% counts toward tutorial participation) Students will pitch their arguments in a 3 minute presentation either in week 11 or 12. Students will be randomly assigned to a week and so all must be ready to present by week 11. Do not read your presentation. Students are expected to talk through the following without reading from notes: Explain the philosophical problem and its significance Explain the two opposing views on the topic Present your own argumentative approach to the problem. A recording of the pitch event will be safely stored on a university computer for up to 12 months as per university policy. While students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. assessment_details.title: Trialogue
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Imagine you are living in the early modern period and have the opportunity to talk philosophy with two of the philosophers we have studied in this course. The two thinkers you choose to write about must have divergent views on one of the topics from the course. Your job is to write a trialogue based on this philosophical encounter between yourself and these two figures. You must capture the dialectic between the opponents, adjudicate between their strongest arguments, and formulate your own answer to the question they are debating based on your own reasoning and evaluation of their arguments. This is an exercise in philosophical storytelling. It should have a good narrative structure and engage the reader both philosophically and from a literary perspective. Maximum word limit : 1500 words (excluding bibliography) . Weight: 30% (Note: Any assignment over 15% must be attempted to obtain a final grade in the course.) Due date: November 9, 2026. 23:59. Submission information : Submit to ‘Trialogue’ Turnitin Assignment under ‘Assessment’ on Blackboard. Obtain a receipt as proof of submission. The School of Historical and Philosophical Inquiry will not accept screenshots as proof work was completed by the due date or as evidence of failed uploads through Turnitin. It is your responsibility to submit to Turnitin by the due date. Any late submission will be subject to late submission penalties. (See section 5.3 of the electronic course profile for further information.) Extensions due to medical emergencies need to be applied for through the School prior to the due date. For information about extensions, see https://my.uq.edu.au/information-and-services/manage-my-program/exams-and-assessment/applying-extension REQUIREMENTS: 1. Students should consult primary sources (texts written by the original historical figures looked at in the course—e.g., Descartes, Spinoza, etc.,) and secondary sources (scholarly analyses of these texts). Good trialogues will often consult 8-10 credible, relevant, and significant sources. Do not list sources in your bibliography that you do not use or cite in the body of your dialogue. 2. The trialogue must come to a conclusion about the topic—it should offer a reasonable justification in support of a thesis. 3. The trialogue should be well-written, checked for spelling and grammar, and must exhibit a high standard of referencing that is used consistently (e.g. APA7). Include in-text references and page numbers for any attributions of ideas and/or quotes. 4. Students must comply with academic misconduct and integrity policies. It is mandatory for all students to complete two academic and misconduct integrity modules to receive a grade in courses (including PHIL2013) in the School of Historical and Philosophical Inquiry. If you have not completed these modules, please do so through Academic Integrity Modules (AIM) . 5. See the Philosophy Criteria Rubric attached under 'Course Files' for more information about the grading criteria and standards. For a guide to writing a philosophical dialogue or trialogue, see https://owlcation.com/humanities/How-to-write-a-Philosophy-Dialogue . learning_activities.topic: Philosophy in transition This seminar focuses on the crucial shifts in thinking that mark the distinction between the philosophies of antiquity and the Middle Ages and the Early Modern period, in particular, the departure from the form/matter and nature/art distinctions of Aristotelianism. An additional tutorial will be offered in this week to students to review argumentation skills, run through the nutshell assignment, and complete the pre-survey for the student-staff partnership. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Metaphysical Themes The philosophers of the 17th and 18th century developed distinctive metaphysical ideas about the building blocks of reality--substances; modes; souls; ideas--and ideas about how things causally interact if they do at all. This week we look at the major metaphysical theories on offer and the reasons behind them. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
No class: Ekka holiday There will be no lectures or tutorials this week, including the Thursday tutorial. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Causation and Agency An examination of different early modern approaches to natural and divine causation and the implications for human agency. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 5 To Week 5 (24 Aug - 30 Aug)
learning_activities.topic: Life An examination of the distinction between living and non-living things under the shift to a mechanical philosophy, as well as debates about functions, systems, and animal consciousness and thought. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Thinking Matter An examination of post-Cartesian debates about the possibility of thinking matter and implications for the nature of the human being. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Human Nature This week examines debates about the nature of the human being--what kind of union exists between the mind and body and what that means for our relationship to each other and the natural world. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Passions and Virtues This week begins the exploration of the relationship between those lynchpins of mind-body union--the passions--and the characteristics of humans that enable it to pursue the good. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Virtue and the passions: Spinoza This seminar consider about the nature and function of the passions and their role in constituting the union of mind and body in the philosophy of Spinoza. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Egoism and Morality This seminar focuses on how thinkers in the early modern period developed ethical theories from their natural philosophical perspectives on the nature and function of the passions and the tension between egoistic and moral motivations to action. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

The equality of the sexes This seminar explores early modern debates about equality between the sexes and their relationship to broader philosophical worldviews in the period. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Political psychology This week compares the political psychologies of Hobbes and Spinoza. We consider the central role played by the passions of hope and fear in Hobbes's and Spinoza's accounts of the constitution of political society, and also consider the rationale for their different proposals regarding the use of these passions as a political tool for governing subjects. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Reception This seminar considers the influence of early modern debates on current debates in moral and political philosophy. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
